mcqs.question: Why do languages like Scala, Rust, and Kotlin deliberately support multiple paradigms instead of committing to one?
options: Because different parts of a typical program (stateful entities, data pipelines, event reactions) fit different paradigms naturally, and forcing all of them into one model usually adds ceremony rather than clarity
Because compilers cannot fully implement a single paradigm without also supporting others
Because multi-paradigm support is required for a language to compile to native machine code
Because it was purely a marketing decision with no technical motivation
mcqs.explanation: Multi-paradigm design reflects that real programs have parts with genuinely different shapes — identity-bearing entities suit OOP, stateless transforms suit FP — and forcing one paradigm everywhere adds ceremony without benefit. It isn't a compiler limitation, unrelated to native code generation, and not merely a marketing choice.

mcqs.question: The imperative, OOP, and functional versions of "compute shipped revenue" all produce the same number. What actually differs between them?
options: Nothing meaningful differs — the three versions are identical in every respect
Only the functional version can produce a correct result; the other two are approximations
Where the logic lives and how it extends — e.g. hidden behind an object's interface, inline in one function, or as an independently testable value-level pipeline
The OOP version always runs asymptotically faster than the other two
mcqs.explanation: The output is identical; what differs is the structure — where the logic is located and how future changes or tests interact with it — which is the actual basis for choosing between them. None of the versions is more "correct," and there's no inherent asymptotic performance difference between them for this computation.

mcqs.question: Why does testing a pure function typically need less setup than testing a method that mutates an object's internal state?
options: Pure functions are always shorter, so there's simply less code to test

A pure function's test is call-with-inputs-assert-output; a mutation-based test needs to construct the object, get it into the right prior state, call the method, then separately assert on the resulting state
Mutation-based methods cannot be unit tested at all
Pure functions never need to be tested since they can't have bugs
mcqs.explanation: The setup gap comes from the mutation-based test needing to construct and inspect state as separate steps, versus the pure function's single input-output check. Mutation-based code is absolutely testable, pure functions can still have bugs, and the difference has nothing to do with code length.

mcqs.question: According to the comparison table, what is a genuine weakness of the declarative paradigm (e.g. SQL)?
options: It cannot express queries involving more than one table
It always requires more code than the equivalent imperative version
Its execution cost is hidden from the source text, making performance harder to control directly than in imperative code
It cannot be used for anything except database queries
mcqs.explanation: Declarative code's brevity hides the execution plan the engine chooses, so performance has to be inspected separately (e.g. via EXPLAIN) rather than read off the source — that's the real trade-off named in the table. It handles multi-table queries fine, is typically shorter not longer, and shows up well beyond databases (configuration, constraint solvers).

mcqs.question: What was the actual problem with early-2000s enterprise Java's "everything must be a class" convention, according to this Subtopic?
options: It made the resulting programs run out of memory more often
Classes are fundamentally incompatible with the Java Virtual Machine
It forced stateless transformations into unnecessary object ceremony, adding indirection and setup cost with no benefit for logic that had no state to bundle
It made it impossible to write unit tests for any class-based code
mcqs.explanation: The concrete cost was structural: wrapping a stateless transformation in a class/factory/container chain adds indirection and testing setup for no payoff, since there's no state to protect via encapsulation. It has nothing to do with memory exhaustion, JVM incompatibility, or making tests impossible — class-based code is very testable.
